title: Given power, they prayed, gave, and stood for good.
subtitle: What believers do when they get a foothold
then: Uthman bin Affan said this was revealed about him and his companions: {idea}expelled for saying our Lord is Allah, then given power{/idea}, they prayed, paid zakah and enjoined good. Umar bin Abdul-Aziz said it applies not only to rulers but also to the ruled.
now: You get the promotion, the bigger house, the say in family decisions. The first thing that shifts is your schedule, and prayer is easy to push aside. {idea}The verse lists what should grow first when you gain ground.{/idea}
old: Once I have more control in life, I will finally relax.
new: More power means more room to pray, give, and do good.
try: Use one bit of influence you have today to encourage something good.

title: If they deny you, Nuh, Aad and Thamud were denied too.
subtitle: Comfort for the Prophet ﷺ in a long line of rejection

row.title: an old pattern
sub: prophets with clear signs were denied

then: Ibn Kathir says Allah here {reward}consoles His Prophet ﷺ{/reward} over his people's denial. Earlier nations rejected their messengers too, despite clear signs and evidence.
now: You tried to share something true and good with your family, and they rolled their eyes at the dinner table. It stings. {idea}The verse puts you in the company of prophets{/idea}: being rejected for the truth is not a sign you were wrong.
old: If people reject what I say, I must have said it badly.
new: Even prophets with clear signs were denied; rejection is not my measure.
try: Say one kind word today to someone who disagreed with you, without reopening the argument.

title: Even Ibrahim and Lut faced their own people's denial.
subtitle: The list continues, closer to home
then: Part of the same consolation to the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Kathir notes these nations denied their prophets {trap}despite all the clear signs{/trap}. Ibrahim, whose House was just described, was among the rejected.
now: Sometimes the hardest pushback comes from the people closest to you: a parent, a sibling, your oldest friends. {idea}Ibrahim, the builder of the House, knew that pain too.{/idea}
old: If my own people do not accept me, maybe I am the problem.
new: The greatest of prophets were refused by their own; I can stay firm and kind.
try: Make dua today, by name, for one family member who does not share your path.

title: I gave them time, then I seized them.
subtitle: Respite is not approval
then: Ibn Kathir explains respite as {idea}I delayed and postponed{/idea}. He cites the Prophet ﷺ: Allah lets the wrongdoer carry on, until when He seizes him He does not let him go.
now: You did the thing you knew was wrong. A week passes, a month. No consequence. It starts to feel normal. {idea}The verse says the quiet is time, not approval{/idea}, and time can be used to turn back.
old: If nothing bad happened after I did wrong, it must not have been that bad.
new: Delay is a mercy to repent, not a sign that wrong is fine.
try: Use today's quiet to repent sincerely for one thing you let slide.

title: A ruined town, a well no one visits, a tall empty palace.
subtitle: What remains of those who did wrong
then: Ibn Kathir describes houses {trap}leveled to their roofs{/trap}, a well once crowded where no one draws water now, and plastered high fortresses that did not protect their owners when the punishment came.
now: You drive past an empty mall, shops boarded, the car park cracked and weedy. It was packed ten years ago. {idea}The verse asks you to read such places as lessons{/idea} about what lasts and what does not.
old: What I build now will keep me safe and remembered.
new: Walls and wealth fade; only what I did for Allah remains.
try: Pass one old or empty building today and remind yourself what truly lasts.

title: It is not the eyes that go blind, but the hearts.
subtitle: Seeing ruins is not the same as learning from them
then: Ibn Kathir says travel here means {idea}both moving through the land and pondering{/idea}. He quotes wise people: give life to your heart with lessons and light it with thought. The truly blind is the one with no insight, even with healthy eyes.
now: You fly abroad, take a hundred photos of old ruins, and come home with only a camera roll. {idea}The verse asks what your heart picked up on the trip{/idea}, not just your phone.
old: I see things clearly because my eyes work fine.
new: Real sight is a heart that takes the lesson from what the eyes see.
try: Look at one thing today and ask: what is Allah teaching me through this?

title: They said hurry up the punishment; His day is a thousand years.
subtitle: Allah's timing and our impatience
then: The deniers mocked the Prophet ﷺ by asking for the punishment to come quickly. Ibn Kathir says {idea}Allah does not hasten{/idea}; He knows He will not miss a thing, even if He delays. Allah never fails His promise.
now: You are waiting for a dua to be answered, checking every week. Someone else is waiting for justice that seems to never come. {reward}The verse says His clock is different, and His promise is never broken.{/reward}
old: If it has not happened yet, it probably will not.
new: Allah's promise is certain; only my sense of time is short.
try: Renew one dua today that you had stopped making because it felt slow.

title: Many towns were given time, and all return to Him.
subtitle: The respite ends, the return is certain
then: Ibn Kathir reads this as following from the previous verse: {idea}He delays and waits{/idea}, then seizes. He also records the Prophet ﷺ saying the poor believers enter Paradise half a day before the rich, five hundred years.
now: Payday, holidays, a new phone. Life feels long and comfortable. {idea}The verse quietly finishes the sentence: and to Me is the return.{/idea} Comfort is not the ending.
old: Things will just keep going the way they are.
new: Every comfortable stretch ends in returning to Allah; I should be ready.
try: End today with a short account: one thing to thank Allah for, one to ask forgiveness for.

title: Say: I am only a clear warner to you.
subtitle: The Prophet's ﷺ role, and what is left to Allah
then: When the deniers demanded the punishment, Allah told the Prophet ﷺ to say this. Ibn Kathir explains: {idea}I warn you, but your reckoning is with Allah{/idea}. He may hasten or delay, and accept the repentance of whoever turns to Him.
now: You warned your friend about a bad deal, clearly and kindly. They went ahead anyway. You keep feeling responsible. {reward}The verse frees you: your job was to warn clearly.{/reward} The rest is with Allah.
old: If someone ignores my advice, I have failed.
new: My part is to speak clearly; the result belongs to Allah.
try: Let go of one person's choice you have been carrying as your own failure.

title: Forgiveness and noble provision for those who believe and act.
subtitle: The good news inside the warning
then: Ibn Kathir says this is {reward}forgiveness for previous bad deeds, and a great reward for a few good deeds{/reward}. Muhammad bin Kab said that noble provision here means Paradise. The warner also brings good news.
now: You look back at the year and see the missed prayers, the sharp words, the wasted nights. It feels too late. {reward}The verse offers forgiveness for the past and generous reward for small good now.{/reward}
old: My past is too messy for any real reward.
new: Allah forgives the past and rewards generously what little good I do now.
try: Do one small good deed today with the hope that Allah multiplies it.

title: Those who worked to defeat His verses.
subtitle: Opposing the message and discouraging others
then: Mujahid said it means trying {trap}to discourage people from following the Prophet ﷺ{/trap}. Ibn Abbas said it means stubbornly resisting the believers. The verse contrasts with the one before it.
now: A cousin starts wearing hijab or going to the mosque, and someone at the family gathering keeps making little jokes. {idea}The verse asks you to check whether you ever discourage someone's turn toward good.{/idea}
old: A bit of teasing about someone's religious change is harmless.
new: Discouraging someone from good is serious; encouraging them is the better effort.
try: Encourage one person today in a good step they are taking.

title: Shaytan throws in confusion, and Allah wipes it away.
subtitle: Every messenger faced interference; Allah secures His verses
then: Ibn Abbas said: when he spoke, Shaytan threw something in, but {idea}Allah cancelled what Shaytan threw in{/idea}. Ibn Kathir mentions a story some commentators told here, but says its chains are weak and he does not regard any of it as sound.
now: You are reading the Quran and a cynical thought pops up, or a clip makes you doubt what you just learned. {reward}The verse says interference is expected{/reward}, and Allah is the one who clears it away and keeps His words firm.
old: If doubts come to me while I read, maybe the message is not solid.
new: Shaytan always throws things in; Allah removes them and keeps His verses firm.
try: When a doubtful thought comes today, seek refuge in Allah and keep reading.

title: The same whisper tests sick hearts and hard hearts.
subtitle: Why Allah lets the confusion appear
then: Ibn Kathir explains the disease as {trap}doubt, shirk, disbelief and hypocrisy{/trap}. Ibn Jurayj said sick hearts are the hypocrites and hard hearts the idolators. The same thing that strengthens one person becomes a trial for another.
now: Two people watch the same video attacking faith. One closes it and asks a scholar. The other forwards it with a laughing emoji. {idea}The video was the same. The hearts were different.{/idea}
old: Doubts come from outside; I am just reacting.
new: The same test reveals what my heart holds, so I tend my heart.
try: Ask Allah today to cure your heart of whatever weakness it carries.

title: Those with knowledge see the truth, and their hearts soften.
subtitle: The same test, the opposite outcome
then: Ibn Kathir says these are people given {idea}beneficial knowledge to tell truth from falsehood{/idea}. They see the Quran is from their Lord and protected, believe it, act on it, and their hearts humble themselves. Allah guides them in this world and the next.
now: You study a little more each week, a tafsir class on your commute, a few pages before bed. One day a doubt that once shook you just passes by. {reward}Knowledge did not make you proud; it made you calm.{/reward}
old: Learning more about my faith will just give me more questions.
new: Beneficial knowledge steadies the heart and makes it humble.
try: Read the tafsir of one verse today, slowly, from a trusted source.
